# Education in Australia: Summary
Education in Australia is regulated and largely funded at the state and territory level, with federal government involvement in funding non-government schools and the tertiary sector. Schooling is compulsory from ages 5-6 to 15-17, depending on jurisdiction. The system comprises preschool (not compulsory, but highly encouraged from age 4, with attendance at 85.7% the year before formal school), primary (generally Years K–6 or K–7), and secondary education (Years 7–12 or 8–12), with a typical school year running from January/February to December. In 2023, 64% of students attended government schools, 19.7% Catholic, and 16.3% independent schools. Schools generally follow the national Australian Curriculum, covering core subjects from English to science, technology, languages, and more.
Australia offers diverse school types, including government, Catholic, and independent schools—many of which are religious or pedagogically distinctive (Montessori, Steiner, Indigenous community schools, and specialist schools for disability and gifted students). Selective schools and bilingual programs exist, especially in New South Wales and the Northern Territory for Indigenous languages. Most students wear uniforms and participate in extra-curricular activities. Attainment of qualifications at Year 12 is available through state-specific certificates or alternatives such as the International Baccalaureate. Tertiary education, including universities and technical/vocational training (TAFE), is predominantly public, highly ranked internationally, and subsidized by government loan programs. Australia is also a major destination for international students. Key issues include ongoing reforms for equitable school funding, educational outcomes disparities—especially for Indigenous students—and efforts to close achievement gaps and improve literacy and numeracy.
